r: SSE 1040 introduces life cycle analysis and systems engineering through basic quantitative methods and classical and modern decision-analysis techniques, applied to sustainable case studies spanning mechanical, civil, and electrical systems. These tasks -- computing life cycle costs, structuring decision matrices, comparing design alternatives -- map onto Analyzing Data or Information and Making Decisions and Solving Problems, activities in the Computer & Mathematical category that observed-usage data shows already dominates both consumer and API traffic. Even granting that exposure, the instrumental need to take this specific course is not eroded at 24 months: it is the entry point of the program's sequence, a listed prerequisite for the SSE 4000 capstone, and it counts toward the ABET-accredited program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor. Foundational scaffolding and the accreditation mandate anchor the rating at Low independent of how competently AI already performs individual life-cycle calculations.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly perform much of the routine life-cycle costing and decision-matrix construction this course teaches, consistent with task-exposure research finding programming and quantitative-analysis skills strongly positively associated with exposure. The instrumental case shifts from execution toward framing which criteria matter, interpreting conflicting model outputs, and judging tradeoffs across mechanical, civil, and electrical alternatives -- capabilities the course still builds through case-study practice. Because SSE 1040 remains a hard prerequisite feeding the capstone and continues to satisfy the ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor, the accreditation-and-foundational cap holds the rating at Medium rather than letting exposed calculation tasks push it toward High. The course is not obsolete; its role narrows toward teaching judgment about AI-generated life-cycle analyses rather than teaching students to produce every analysis unaided from scratch.

A decade out, AI is plausibly embedded throughout systems-engineering workflows, generating life-cycle cost models and decision analyses on demand with capability that the METR/Epoch trend of rapidly lengthening autonomous task horizons suggests could be substantial by 2036. Yet the accreditation architecture is slow-moving: absent an ABET curriculum change, the program still needs roughly the same engineering-topic and math/science credit-hour floor, and SSE 1040 still gates entry to the capstone sequence. The rating holds at Medium, capped by foundational scaffolding and program mandate rather than by task difficulty. The genuine uncertainty is how thoroughly automated life-cycle analysis becomes and whether accreditors eventually redefine the credit-hour requirement, not whether an introductory decision-analysis course remains instrumentally tied to the accredited degree in the near term.
SSE 1040.d: Students in this course are introduced to life cycle analysis and systems engineering using principles and applications of systems analysis, life cycle cost analysis and basic quantitative methods. Classical and modern decision analysis techniques are employed for evaluating case studies in sustainable systems of mechanical, civil and electrical engineering.

r: SSE 1215 teaches solid-modeling fundamentals, geometric construction, multi-view projection, section views, and dimensioning using CAD software -- applied tasks that map closely to Interacting With Computers and Drafting, Laying Out, and Specifying Technical Devices, Parts, and Equipment. Text-to-CAD and generative modeling tools already exist and are improving, and task-exposure research classifies programming-adjacent, tool-mediated work as positively associated with exposure. Still, at 24 months the instrumental need to take the course is not eroded: dimensioning conventions, spatial reasoning, and section-view judgment are hands-on competencies students build through repeated CAD practice, not yet reliably delegated to AI, and the course contributes to the ABET-accredited program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor. Foundational tool literacy for later design coursework and the accreditation mandate together hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI-assisted CAD generation will plausibly draft solid models and multi-view projections from natural-language or sketch input competently enough that productivity gains resembling the roughly 56% faster task completion observed with GitHub Copilot on adjacent coding work are a reasonable analog for modeling throughput. The instrumental case narrows toward verifying that a generated model satisfies dimensioning standards, tolerances, and section-view correctness rather than constructing every view by hand. Because the course still seeds spatial and drafting literacy used throughout the design curriculum and counts toward the ABET credit-hour floor, the rating rises only to Medium rather than High. Execution automates faster than the underlying spatial-reasoning competence the course cultivates, and the accreditation structure keeps the course in the required sequence.

A decade out, generative CAD tools plausibly produce publication-quality solid models directly from specifications, and the manual-construction rationale for this course is substantially eroded under a central capability-growth scenario emphasizing fast progress in autonomous task-completion horizons. But verifying that an AI-generated model is dimensionally sound, manufacturable, and standards-compliant still draws on the drafting literacy this course builds, and the ABET-accredited program's credit-hour floor for engineering-topic content persists absent a formal curriculum revision. The rating holds at Medium, capped by the accreditation mandate and by the course's residual role in developing spatial judgment. The uncertainty concerns how much of the modeling workflow shifts to review-only verification work rather than hands-on construction, not whether the course keeps a foothold in the required engineering-technology sequence through 2036.
SSE 1215.d: In this course students study solid modeling fundamentals, geometric constructions, multi-view projections, section views, and dimensioning using adequate CAD software.

r: SSE 2100 covers DC and AC circuit analysis, network theorems, power and complex power, phasors, impedance, and digital systems, with applied tasks mapping to Analyzing Data or Information and Interacting With Computers as students compute circuit responses and reason about electronic-system behavior. Circuit computation is a well-defined, symbolic task that current AI performs competently, consistent with task-exposure research linking quantitative and programming-adjacent work to higher exposure. But confirming that a predicted circuit response matches real hardware requires the trained human judgment this course builds -- a genuine verification burden -- and the course is foundational scaffolding within an ABET-accredited electrical-engineering-technology sequence. At 24 months, the instrumental need is not eroded: AI solves the equations, but the course grounds hardware reasoning and satisfies the program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor.

By 2031, AI will fluently perform circuit analysis and simulation, weakening the rationale for working every phasor or impedance calculation by hand, an erosion pattern task-exposure research would predict given circuit math's resemblance to other highly-exposed quantitative work. But real circuit behavior can diverge from prediction, and diagnosing that gap against physical measurement demands exactly the kind of expert verification the jagged-frontier findings warn is easy to get wrong when trust in AI output is miscalibrated. Foundational scaffolding for later electrical coursework and the ABET-relevant credit-hour floor cap the erosion at Medium rather than allowing it toward High. The rating rises from Low to Medium: analytical execution increasingly automates, but hardware-verification competence and program mandate keep the course instrumentally necessary.

A decade out, AI plausibly handles circuit analysis and much preliminary electronic-system design automatically, and the hand-calculation rationale for this course is largely eroded under an aggressive capability scenario consistent with the METR/Epoch trend of rapidly lengthening autonomous task horizons. Electrical-systems work nonetheless retains an embodied component -- measuring real circuits, troubleshooting discrepancies between simulation and hardware -- and the ABET-accredited program's structural requirement for foundational engineering-topic credit hours persists absent accreditor action. The rating holds at Medium, capped by foundational role and verification burden rather than falling to Low or rising to High. The genuine uncertainty is how much routine circuit design and diagnosis shifts to AI-assisted workflows by 2036, not whether foundational circuit competence remains instrumentally tied to the accredited electrical-systems sequence in the meantime.
SSE 2100.d: In this course, students study DC and AC circuits, including electric components, classic network theorems, electric power and complex power, phasor, impedance, digital system, etc. The application and development of electronic systems is also discussed.

r: SSE 2150 covers static equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies, section properties, internal forces in statically determinate trusses and beams, friction, and virtual work -- analytical tasks mapping to Analyzing Data or Information and Making Decisions and Solving Problems as students compute reactions, internal forces, and equilibrium conditions. This is well-structured symbolic and numeric problem-solving, a category observed-usage data shows already concentrated in the Computer & Mathematical usage class. Still, at 24 months the instrumental need to take the course is not eroded: SSE 2150 is a required prerequisite for both Strength of Materials and Mechanics of Dynamic Systems, making it critical scaffolding for the ABET-accredited sequence, and it satisfies part of the program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor. Foundational role and accreditation mandate hold the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI will plausibly solve truss and beam equilibrium problems, compute section properties, and generate free-body diagrams reliably, an erosion consistent with task-exposure research's finding that quantitative, well-specified problem-solving is strongly associated with exposure. The instrumental case shifts toward the conceptual grounding students need to set up problems correctly, interpret AI-generated solutions, and catch sign errors or unrealistic support assumptions before they propagate into later structural coursework. Because SSE 2150 remains a hard prerequisite gating both Strength of Materials and Dynamics, and continues to count toward the ABET credit-hour floor, foundational scaffolding caps the erosion at Medium. The rating rises from Low: routine statics computation increasingly automates, but the gating role in the accredited sequence keeps the course necessary.

A decade out, AI plausibly performs statics analysis end to end with high reliability, consistent with a central-case capability trajectory where symbolic mechanics problems fall well inside the model's competence frontier. Yet SSE 2150's structural position as the prerequisite substrate for both the strength-of-materials and dynamics sequences persists in the central case, and the ABET-accredited program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor does not relax without formal accreditor revision, which moves slowly. The rating holds at Medium, capped by foundational role and institutional lock-in rather than by residual task difficulty. The uncertainty concerns how mechanics is taught once computation is fully automatable, whether emphasis shifts entirely to conceptual setup and verification, not whether the course remains instrumentally tied to the required sequence through 2036.
SSE 2150.d: In this course, students study the principles of mechanics of static systems in two- and three-dimensions: static equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies; section properties; internal forces in statically determinate trusses and beams; friction; and virtual work.

r: SSE 3100 has students describe complex real-world engineering systems with mathematical concepts, working in teams to tackle engineering application problems by applying theory learned in prior coursework. The tasks map to Analyzing Data or Information and Coordinating the Work and Activities of Others, since the course explicitly runs through team-based problem-solving rather than solo computation -- a collaborative, in-person dimension that moderates the otherwise-high exposure of the underlying mathematics. AI can already assist with formulating and solving mathematical models, consistent with task-exposure research's finding of strong positive exposure for quantitative work, but the course's team framing and its role applying material from the MTH 3420 prerequisite within the ABET-accredited sequence keep the instrumental need intact. The rating stays Low at 24 months, anchored by the accreditation mandate and applied-teamwork structure.

By 2031, AI will plausibly formulate mathematical models for engineering systems fluently on its own, weakening the rationale for students to construct models from scratch -- an erosion the task-exposure literature would predict given how strongly quantitative modeling correlates with exposure. The instrumental case shifts toward the team-based judgment the course is built around: choosing which real-world features to abstract into a model, negotiating modeling choices with teammates, and evaluating whether an AI-generated model captures the engineering problem correctly. Because the course continues to satisfy the ABET-accredited program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor and retains its collaborative-application structure, the erosion is capped at Medium rather than High. The rating rises from Low: model construction increasingly automates, but framing judgment and program mandate keep the course necessary.

A decade out, AI plausibly generates and refines mathematical models of engineering systems with high proficiency under an aggressive central-case capability trajectory, substantially eroding the construction rationale for this small, application-focused course. The ABET-accredited program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor nonetheless persists absent formal accreditor revision, and the course's team-based framing -- applying and negotiating modeling choices collaboratively -- retains a structure not fully replicated by solitary AI use. The rating holds at Medium, capped by accreditation mandate and the collaborative-application format rather than by the underlying mathematics remaining hard for AI. The uncertainty concerns how much team-based modeling pedagogy itself changes once individual model construction is largely automated, not whether the course keeps its place in the required curriculum through 2036.
SSE 3100.d: In this course, students develop the ability to describe complex, real-world, engineering systems with mathematical concepts. Mathematical modeling is presented through engineering application problems that students tackle by working in teams and applying the theory they have learnt in other courses.

r: SSE 3135 develops constitutive relationships for materials under axial, torsion, shear, and bending loads, beam-deflection and column-buckling theory, and pairs that theory with laboratory time measuring engineering properties on physical equipment. The analytical tasks map to Analyzing Data or Information, while the lab component maps to Inspecting Equipment, Structures, or Materials -- a hands-on measurement activity task-exposure frameworks treat as lower-exposure than pure calculation. Verifying that a material's measured behavior matches predicted constitutive relationships requires trained judgment the course builds, and SSE 3135 is a required prerequisite for Modeling Structural Systems within the ABET-accredited sequence. At 24 months, the instrumental need is not eroded: AI can solve the governing equations, but the course grounds the lab-verification competence and hard prerequisite role the curriculum depends on.

By 2031, AI will fluently derive stress-strain relationships and solve deflection and buckling problems, eroding the hand-calculation rationale in a pattern task-exposure research would predict for well-specified engineering mathematics. But interpreting laboratory measurements -- strain-gauge readings, load-test data that deviates from theory -- and diagnosing why real material behavior departs from the model remains a genuine verification burden with safety implications, exactly the kind of jagged-frontier gap where miscalibrated trust in AI predictions is costly and failures can be non-obvious until a structure is loaded. Foundational scaffolding for Modeling Structural Systems and the ABET-relevant credit-hour floor cap the erosion at Medium. The rating rises from Low: calculation automates, but lab-verification competence and the course's gating role in the accredited sequence keep it instrumentally necessary.

A decade out, AI plausibly automates most constitutive-relationship calculation and much deflection and buckling analysis, and the computational rationale for the course is substantially eroded under an aggressive capability scenario for symbolic engineering mathematics. Physical material testing and diagnosing bench-versus-prediction discrepancies remain partly embodied work, however, and SSE 3135's role as the required gateway to Modeling Structural Systems persists in the central case, alongside an ABET credit-hour floor that changes only on an accreditation cycle. The rating holds at Medium, capped by foundational role and lab-verification burden rather than falling toward Low or rising toward High. The uncertainty is how much bench measurement itself becomes automated by 2036, not whether the prerequisite relationship and accreditation mandate keep the course structurally necessary.
SSE 3135.d: Students in this course are introduced to the fundamentals in the strength and deformation of engineering materials. Students focus on the development of constitutive relationships of materials under axial, torsion, transverse shear and bending loading conditions, and the engineering applications in the first part of the course. Students are introduced to beam-deflection and column-buckling theories and engineering solutions in the second part of the course. Students use laboratory time to enhance the knowledge and theories developed in the class and to use different equipment measuring engineering properties of various materials.

r: SSE 3160 introduces kinematics and kinetics of particles and rigid bodies with engineering applications, plus vibration systems -- analytical tasks mapping to Analyzing Data or Information and Making Decisions and Solving Problems as students derive equations of motion and analyze vibrating systems. Like statics, this is well-structured symbolic and numeric mechanics, a category observed-usage data shows concentrated in already-heavy Computer & Mathematical usage. At 24 months, the instrumental need to take the course is not eroded: SSE 3160 requires SSE 2150 as a prerequisite and builds mechanics competence used across the ABET-accredited mechanical and civil tracks, while satisfying part of the program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor. AI can already assist with equations of motion, but the course grounds the modeling judgment and prerequisite chain the curriculum depends on.

By 2031, AI will plausibly solve equations of motion and analyze vibration systems fluently, an erosion consistent with task-exposure research linking symbolic, quantitative mechanics to strong positive exposure. The instrumental case shifts toward correctly framing a dynamic system -- choosing coordinates, identifying constraints, deciding which vibration modes matter -- and toward critically checking AI-generated solutions for physically implausible results before they inform later design work. Because the course sits within the ABET-accredited sequence and continues to satisfy the engineering-topic credit-hour floor, and because it feeds downstream mechanics-dependent coursework across the program, the erosion is capped at Medium rather than High. The rating rises from Low: routine dynamics computation increasingly automates, but framing and verification judgment, plus program mandate, keep the course necessary.

A decade out, AI plausibly performs dynamics analysis, including multi-body and vibration problems, with high reliability under a central capability-growth trajectory reflecting rapid gains in autonomous task-completion horizons, substantially eroding the case for manual computation. But the ABET-accredited program's credit-hour floor for engineering-topic content persists absent formal accreditor revision, and SSE 3160 remains prerequisite-linked mechanics content feeding later coursework in the sequence. The rating holds at Medium, capped by institutional lock-in and the course's continuing role in the required mechanics progression rather than by residual computational difficulty. The genuine uncertainty is how dynamics instruction reorganizes once computation is largely automated, toward framing, simulation interpretation, and verification, not whether the course keeps its structural place in the accredited curriculum through 2036.
SSE 3160.d: In this course, students are introduced to dynamics systems, including kinematics, and kinetics of particles and rigid bodies with engineering applications. Students also study the vibration systems in engineering applications.

r: SSE 3175 teaches structural modeling for analysis and design, focusing on how components interact and behave within a structural system, the evolution of structural-analysis methods, and the range of analysis types and their interactions. These tasks map to Analyzing Data or Information and Thinking Creatively as students build and interpret structural models -- work that current structural-analysis and simulation software already assists heavily, and that observed-usage data would classify within the dominant Computer & Mathematical usage category. At 24 months, the instrumental need is not eroded: the course requires Strength of Materials as a prerequisite, occupies a later position in the ABET-accredited mechanics-to-structures sequence, and counts toward the program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor. The rating stays Low, anchored by prerequisite structure and accreditation mandate rather than by task difficulty alone.

By 2031, AI-assisted structural modeling and simulation tools will plausibly generate candidate structural models and run comparative analyses efficiently, consistent with task-exposure research's finding that quantitative modeling work is strongly positively associated with exposure. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying which structural-system interactions matter, selecting appropriate analysis methods, and judging whether a generated model's behavior is physically sound -- skills GDPval-style evaluations against real deliverables suggest AI still falls short of full human-expert reliability on. Because the course remains gated behind Strength of Materials and continues to satisfy the ABET-accredited program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor, the erosion is capped at Medium. The rating rises from Low: routine model construction increasingly automates, but framing and verification judgment, plus program mandate, keep the course necessary.

A decade out, AI plausibly generates and iterates structural models with substantial sophistication, and the manual-construction rationale for this course is significantly eroded under a central capability scenario emphasizing fast progress in autonomous task-completion horizons and compute growth. But the ABET-accredited program's credit-hour floor for engineering-topic content persists absent a formal accreditation revision, and the course's position downstream of Strength of Materials keeps it embedded in the required sequence. The rating holds at Medium, capped by accreditation mandate rather than by residual difficulty in the modeling tasks themselves. The uncertainty concerns how much of structural-system verification and safety judgment can be delegated to AI by 2036 without expert oversight, not whether the course retains its place in the accredited curriculum.
SSE 3175.d: In this course, students study the modeling for structural analysis and design. It focuses on the interaction of the components and their behavior within a structural system. The basic concepts of structural modeling are introduced first, followed by the evolution of structural analysis, and then the analysis methods and types are presented, along with the discussion of interactions within structural systems.

r: SSE 3500 pairs hands-on instruction with project work in which students design and implement a sustainable community project addressing an underrepresented community's basic engineering needs, applying Appropriate Design concepts and development-implementation strategy grounded in community-development methodologies. These tasks map to Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships and Coordinating the Work and Activities of Others -- real-time, in-person, contextual work that task-exposure research places among the least-exposed categories, in contrast to the writing and programming tasks it finds strongly positively exposed. Verifying that a community-engineering solution actually fits local needs, resources, and culture requires embedded human judgment no remote AI system supplies. At 24 months the instrumental need is fully intact: the embodied, relational core of the course -- direct engagement with a community and hands-on implementation -- is not delegable.

By 2031, AI will plausibly assist with drafting project proposals, researching development methodologies, and summarizing Appropriate Design frameworks, augmenting the desk-research portion of the course. That leaves untouched the defining applied work: face-to-face community engagement, contextual needs assessment, and hands-on project implementation, which task-exposure research continues to classify as low-exposure relative to writing and programming work. Verification burden stays high -- a design that looks appropriate on paper can fail badly against local context, materials, or culture, and only embedded human judgment catches that before implementation. Diffusion data shows AI adoption remains uneven across firms generally, and community-engineering practice is far from a setting where remote AI assistance substitutes for on-the-ground work. The rating stays Low: augmenting background research does not erode the embodied, relational core of this course.

A decade out, even under an aggressive central-case capability scenario, the interpersonal and embodied core of humanitarian engineering -- building trust with a community, adapting a design to on-the-ground constraints, physically implementing a project -- sits outside the task categories where capability growth translates into instrumental substitution. Task-exposure research's consistent finding that interpersonal and manual-context work resists automation, together with macro-level evidence that productivity effects from AI diffusion remain modest over a decade, supports holding this course at Low rather than projecting erosion toward Medium. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much AI reshapes the research and documentation students do before entering the field, not whether direct community engagement and hands-on implementation remain instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low with the course's embodied, relational character as the binding constraint throughout.
SSE 3500.d: In this course, students are introduced to humanitarian engineering through hands-on instruction and project work in tandem with lectures. Students design and implement a sustainable community project that helps an underrepresented community to meet the population's basic engineering needs. This project is based on knowledge of relevant community development methodologies that students are introduced to through lecture. Students learn to apply Appropriate Design concepts, as well as development implementation strategy with respect to sustainability, and design for community. Students compare and contrast engineering for developing community systems strategies with the traditional design process.

r: SSE 4000 is the program's capstone, applying advanced life-cycle analysis, quantitative methods, engineering economics, and classical and modern decision-analysis methods to sustainability-guided case studies across mechanical, civil, and electrical systems, using optimization techniques for detailed analysis. These tasks map to Analyzing Data or Information and Making Decisions and Solving Problems, squarely within the Computer & Mathematical usage category that observed-usage data shows already dominant. At 24 months, the instrumental need to take this course is not eroded: it requires SSE 1040 and CET 3120 as prerequisites, sits as the terminal synthesis course of the ABET-accredited sequence, and satisfies part of the program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor. The capstone integrates and demonstrates competencies across the degree; AI assisting individual calculations does not remove the requirement to complete it.

By 2031, AI will plausibly perform much of the optimization, life-cycle costing, and decision-matrix construction this capstone exercises, consistent with task-exposure research's finding that quantitative-analysis skills are strongly positively associated with exposure and with productivity studies showing substantial speedups on similarly structured professional tasks. The instrumental case shifts toward synthesizing sustainability tradeoffs across disciplines, defending design decisions, and critically evaluating AI-generated optimization outputs for realism -- exactly the integrative judgment a capstone is meant to certify. Because SSE 4000 remains the terminal, accreditation-anchored synthesis course requiring SSE 1040 and CET 3120, and continues to count toward the ABET credit-hour floor, the erosion caps at Medium. The rating rises from Low: routine analysis automates, but the capstone's integrative and accreditation-anchored role persists.

A decade out, AI is plausibly deeply embedded in sustainable-systems workflows, generating candidate designs and life-cycle optimizations rapidly under a central capability-growth trajectory. But a capstone's institutional function -- certifying that a student can integrate and defend decisions across mechanical, civil, and electrical sustainability tradeoffs -- does not disappear simply because component calculations automate, and the ABET-accredited program's credit-hour floor persists absent formal accreditor revision. The rating holds at Medium, capped by the course's terminal-synthesis role and the accreditation mandate rather than by residual task difficulty. The uncertainty concerns how capstone assessment itself evolves under pervasive AI, whether it shifts toward evaluating judgment about AI-generated designs, not whether the course remains structurally required to complete the accredited degree through 2036.
SSE 4000.d: ln this course, students study advanced theories and applications of sustainable systems engineering, life cycle analysis, quantitative methods and engineering economics, guided by sustainability principles. Classical and modern decision analysis methods are employed for evaluating case studies in terms of mechanical, civil and electrical engineering using content optimization techniques for detailed analysis and application.

r: Geotechnical engineering combines soil-mechanics calculation with hands-on laboratory testing: sieve analysis, Atterberg limits, hydraulic conductivity, and shear strength measurement. Consolidation and settlement calculations, classification lookups, and report drafting are AI-assistable tasks, but running the bench tests and reading instrument behavior require physical presence and manual dexterity that task-exposure research places in the low-exposure manual-work category. Verification burden is high: interpreting inconsistent subsurface data and judging shear-strength results against real soil variability demands trained judgment, since a wrong reading feeds directly into foundation and retaining-wall design. The course's engineering-topic credit hours also count toward the program's ABET accreditation floor. At 24 months the instrumental need to physically run and interpret these tests is intact; AI accelerates calculation but does not replace the lab.

By 2031, AI tools will fluidly perform consolidation, settlement, and bearing-capacity calculations and draft geotechnical report language, further eroding the pure-computation rationale for the course. But the bench work — sieve analysis, Atterberg limits, hydraulic conductivity, shear testing — remains embodied, and interpreting ambiguous or inconsistent field data against site-specific soil behavior stays a genuine verification burden; the jagged-frontier finding shows AI users are notably less accurate outside a model's competence zone when trust is miscalibrated, which matters when subsurface conditions vary. The ABET-accredited program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor keeps the course structurally required regardless of computational automation. The rating stays Low: calculation exposure rises, but the embodied lab core and safety-critical verification demand keep the instrumental case for taking the course intact.

A decade out, capability-trend evidence suggests AI systems handle substantially more of the analytical workflow, and semi-automated or remote-sensing-assisted lab and field techniques may reduce some hands-on burden. Routine calculation, classification, and documentation tasks are then heavily automated. But geotechnical design remains safety-critical — a misjudged bearing capacity or slope-stability estimate has severe failure consequences — so verifying AI-generated geotechnical analysis against physical soil behavior still requires trained human judgment, and diffusion research indicates firm-level AI adoption still lags capability even at this horizon. The ABET engineering-topic floor continues to lock the course into the accredited curriculum. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting real erosion of routine analysis alongside persistent verification burden and accreditation lock-in; how much of the physical lab itself automates by 2036 is genuinely uncertain.
SSE 4160.d: Students in this course are introduced to the basic principles of soil behavior and their use in geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering. This course covers soil formation, soil characterization and classification, engineering properties of soil, compaction, fluid flow in soil, stresses in soil, consolidation and settlement, shear strength, and lateral earth pressures. Students are introduced to soil improvement and remediation strategies and the design of earth retaining structures. This course contains a laboratory that covers common geotechnical tests such as sieve analysis, Atterberg limits, hydraulic conductivity, and soil shear strength.

r: This course covers the role of engineering in development, sustainability-oriented planning, development economics, and frameworks for large- and small-scale development projects in medium- to high-risk, low-resilience communities, plus leadership skills for uncertain decision environments. Much of the graded work is analytical writing and framework application — drafting development strategy documents, applying planning tools — tasks that task-exposure research associates positively with AI exposure, and Anthropic Economic Index usage data shows writing and office-style tasks are already prominent in observed use. The course carries no general-studies designation, so no gen-ed transfer mandate applies, but its engineering-topic credit hours count toward the program's ABET accreditation floor. At 24 months the instrumental need to build development-strategy competence directly is intact; AI drafts documents but doesn't substitute for the judgment the course teaches.

By 2031, AI will competently draft development-strategy documents, synthesize development-economics frameworks, and generate planning analyses, substantially eroding the rationale for students to produce this content unassisted — consistent with observed automation-leaning usage patterns in professional writing and analysis tasks. What resists automation is judgment under genuine uncertainty: assessing risk and resilience in specific communities with unfamiliar social, political, and economic systems, and making leadership decisions when information is incomplete and stakes are real. The ABET engineering-topic credit-hour floor keeps the course structurally required within the accredited curriculum even as the accreditation body sets no gen-ed transfer mandate of its own. The rating rises to Medium: document-production tasks automate substantially, but contextual judgment and accreditation-driven credit requirements keep the course instrumentally necessary.

Ten years out, AI systems will likely generate sophisticated development-strategy frameworks and scenario analyses, and firm-level diffusion data suggests such tools become progressively normalized in planning workflows even though adoption still lags raw capability at even a longer horizon. The instrumental residue narrows toward exercising leadership judgment in ambiguous, high-risk community contexts, coordinating stakeholders in real project settings, and critically evaluating AI-generated development plans for a specific social and political setting that AI cannot fully model from training data alone. The ABET-accredited program's credit-hour floor continues to require engineering-topic coursework of this kind regardless of how much document generation automates. The rating holds Medium, capped by that accreditation lock rather than by task protection alone. Considerable uncertainty remains about whether decision-analysis judgment itself becomes substantially AI-augmentable at scale by 2036, which would further erode the instrumental case.
SSE 4200.d: In this course, students are introduced to the role of engineering in development, and they examine how actions lead to intended and unintended consequences. Emphasis is placed on sustainability principles with regards to planning and design, and the key components of development economics. Students study development strategy on large, modern world scale and also for communities where the social, political, and economic systems differ from those most commonly experienced by engineers in the developed world. The students are also introduced to a framework and guidelines for conducting both large- and small-scale development projects. The course addresses analysis of communities in medium- to high-risk and low-resilience environments. The framework combines concepts and tools that have been traditionally used by development agencies and other tools more specifically used in engineering project management. Finally, students are introduced to the various leadership skills necessary to make decisions in complex and uncertain environments.

r: This course teaches stochastic design methods — basic probability concepts, the evolution of probabilistic design, and Monte Carlo simulation applied to structural analysis and design. This is precisely the quantitative, computation-heavy work that task-exposure research flags as strongly exposed: mathematicians and quantitative analysts rank among the most AI-exposed occupations, and Monte Carlo methods are formalizable simulation routines AI tools already execute. But verification burden is real: a probabilistic design output feeds structural safety margins, so checking that a simulation's assumptions and distributions are correctly specified requires expert oversight, a high-error-cost, non-obvious-failure situation. The course's engineering-topic hours also count toward the ABET accreditation floor. At 24 months the instrumental need to learn to run and interpret these simulations directly is intact despite high raw exposure, because of the verification demand.

By 2031, AI will fluently set up and run Monte Carlo simulations and probabilistic design calculations, sharply eroding the execution rationale — consistent with the strong positive exposure evidence documented for quantitative-analysis occupations such as mathematicians and quantitative analysts. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying correct probability distributions, catching flawed assumptions embedded in an AI-generated simulation, and judging whether stochastic design outputs are trustworthy enough for structural applications; the jagged-frontier finding that users are markedly less accurate outside a model's competence zone, with miscalibrated trust, underscores why this verification skill still matters here. The ABET credit-hour floor keeps probabilistic methods coursework structurally required in the accredited curriculum regardless. The rating rises to Medium: simulation execution largely automates, but assumption-verification competence and accreditation lock-in together prevent full erosion of the instrumental case.

A decade out, capability-trend evidence on rapidly lengthening AI task-time horizons suggests probabilistic design workflows, from distribution selection through simulation to sensitivity analysis, become largely AI-executable end to end with minimal human input. The residual instrumental case narrows to catching AI-generated simulations that encode wrong assumptions about variable distributions or correlations — a genuine verification role given the high cost of an undetected error in a safety-relevant structural design decision. The ABET-accredited program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor continues to structurally require this content regardless of how much routine execution automates by then. The rating holds Medium, capped by that accreditation mandate rather than by task protection. It remains genuinely uncertain whether verification of stochastic design will still require the depth of hand-computation this course currently teaches, or only a lighter conceptual treatment, by 2036.
SSE 4300.d: In this course, students study engineering design methods that account for the stochastic nature of the design variables and provide means to quantify the inherent risk of a design. The students are introduced to basic concepts of stochastics, followed by the evolution of the probabilistic design, after which the design methods are discussed with emphasis on the Monte Carlo simulation and its applications to structural analysis and design.

r: This course teaches risk and decision analysis for project-level engineering decisions involving multiple variables and complex, often competing risks, using Monte Carlo analysis and multicriteria decision methods, with a collaborative term project. The quantitative core — running Monte Carlo risk models, structuring multicriteria comparisons — is the kind of formal analytical work task-exposure research associates with high AI exposure. But project-level decisions carry real consequences (cost, schedule, safety) and the verification burden is high: a flawed risk model or miscalibrated decision weighting is a non-obvious failure with significant downstream cost, and the collaborative term project retains an interpersonal, real-time coordination component. The course's engineering-topic hours count toward the ABET accreditation floor. At 24 months, the instrumental need to learn to build and defend these analyses directly remains intact.

By 2031, AI will competently run Monte Carlo risk simulations and multicriteria decision frameworks and draft supporting analysis narratives — professional-writing productivity research shows large time savings alongside quality gains on this kind of analytical document work. What resists automation is structuring which risks and criteria matter for a specific project, weighting them under genuine uncertainty, and catching a flawed AI-generated risk model before it drives a costly project decision — a verification burden with real stakes. Team-based coordination on the term project also retains an interpersonal element. The ABET credit-hour floor keeps decision-and-risk-analysis coursework structurally required in the accredited program. The rating rises to Medium: model execution and drafting automate substantially, but problem-framing judgment, verification burden, and accreditation lock-in hold the course in place.

Ten years out, AI-assisted risk and decision analysis tools will likely be pervasive in project engineering workflows, and diffusion research suggests firm-level adoption keeps expanding even though it still lags raw capability. The instrumental residue concentrates on framing which risks and decision criteria are relevant to a specific, high-stakes project and verifying that an AI-generated risk-and-decision analysis is sound before it informs real resource commitments — a persistent verification burden given the cost of an undetected flaw. The ABET-accredited program's engineering-topic credit-hour floor continues to require this coursework regardless of how much modeling automates. The rating holds Medium, capped by accreditation lock-in and verification demand rather than by task protection. Whether problem-framing itself becomes substantially AI-assisted by 2036 remains genuinely uncertain.
SSE 4700.d: Students learn the fundamental principles and practical techniques of risk and decision analysis in this course. The class is oriented toward project-level decisions where multiple variables and complex risks are present. The course introduces students to Monte Carlo analyses, and various types of multicriteria decision analyses. Students collaborate in a larger term project. Theatre
